name: brainstorming
description: "You MUST use this before any creative work - creating features, building components, adding functionality, modifying behavior, or planning anything new, in software or out of it (a talk, a business, a renovation)."
---

# Brainstorming

You are very good at building. You build what you believe your human
partner wants, and that belief is usually thinner than it feels. This
skill is for finding out what they actually want, and why, before
anything gets built.

People often haven't finished working out what they want. Good questions
help them think it through. When you understand the why, you make the
hundred decisions they never mention the way they would have made them.

## First: What Do You Actually Know?

Before you reply, ask yourself: what do I know about what they want, and
why?

- **Everything that matters is in the request** ("make the icon cornflower
  blue"). This is a quick, clear task. Do it, and say what you did.
- **Something non-trivial is missing.** Start the conversation.

Before you start implementing, you must, in order:

1. Lay out the approaches in a message of their own, and have your
   human partner pick one (see Lay out the approaches).
2. Write the design doc, short or full (see Size the Work).
3. Get their approval of that doc.
4. Invoke the superpowers:writing-plans skill.

Two things aren't implementing: a spike they said yes to (see Spike to
feel things out), and doing what they asked once they've opted out of
the questions.

## Look Before You Ask

In an existing project, or when they've given you context (a spec, a plan,
a handoff, files they pointed at, earlier conversation), dig in before your
first message. Read what they referred to and the code or material it
connects to, and keep reading until you can explain how the relevant
parts work today and what this change would touch. Never ask what the
project or their context already answers.

## Your First Message

Move the work forward, with one of these:

- **They've already said what they want** (a spec, a plan, a detailed
  request): aim for about 200 words for the whole message. Echo their
  request back in your own words, so they can see whether you've got its
  shape: what they want, who it's for, and why, as far as they've said.
  Add what you found that bears on it: how the relevant parts work today
  and what the change would touch. If you found something they may not
  have considered that would change what they're asking for or how it
  has to be built, like a constraint, a conflict, or a cheaper path, say
  so plainly. How to build it comes later, once you understand what they
  want (see Lay out the approaches). End with one line inviting
  corrections, then one question about what they want: the thing their
  request leaves open whose answer would most change what gets built.
  Specs are often incomplete, so confirm before you build on one.
- **They haven't:** one open question, in their own terms, about the
  biggest thing their request leaves unsettled. Say why you're asking:
  what the answer would change about what you build. For "a website for
  my bakery": "If it's mostly for people deciding whether to stop by,
  I'd lead with hours and what's in the case today; taking orders is a
  different site. What do you want someone to do when they land on it?"

How the message ends depends on whether their message asked for
brainstorming:

- **They asked for it** (by name, by invoking it, or by asking for a
  design discussion): end with your question. They want this
  conversation.
- **They didn't:** they may not want a conversation at all. After your
  question, add a light, one-line offer to just get going instead, like
  "Or if you'd rather I just dive in, say so." If they take you up on
  it, this skill is done: state any significant how-it-gets-made choice
  (platform, language, medium) in one plain line, then do what they
  asked through the normal workflow.

That's the whole message.

## The Conversation

Each message ends with one question: a single sentence with no list of
example answers hanging off it. Use plain language, pitched just a little
above where your human partner is. Match their vocabulary; never use
process jargon. You never need to quote this skill to your human
partner.

Be clear and concise. Lead with what matters. Avoid jargon. When you
report what you found, give them the most important findings and offer
the rest.

**Get them describing.** Open questions come first. Their own words carry
intent that your options can't. Offer a short menu only when they're
stuck. When they say "just guess" or "what do you think?", propose
something concrete.

**How it gets made.** Every project rests on choices about medium, tools,
materials, and resources: the platform, programming language, and
libraries for an app; the medium for a piece of art. Find out early which
of those choices they want to make, which they're handing to you, and what
they already have to work with. Someone with strong views or skills will
want to talk it through. Someone counting on you needs sensible defaults,
said in plain words. When there's existing work, build on what it already
uses. Any choice you make goes in the design as your call, never as
something they agreed to.

**Ground to cover.** This is territory, not a script. Never read these
out as questions:

- what kind of thing this is, and what makes it special
- why now, and what success looks like to them
- goals, non-goals, and anti-goals (what would make this a failure even
  if it technically works)
- prior art: what they've seen elsewhere, loved or hated
- current state: what exists now, what they've tried
- the details they care about

**Make every question specific** to their project and what they've told
you. Ask Socratically, the way a sharp colleague would: build each
question on their last answer or on something you found, so it helps
them think through a consequence or a case they may have missed
("Voting closes before the meeting, and two members joined this month.
Does someone who joins mid-round get a vote?"). When the reason isn't
already plain, say what you're hoping to learn or what the answer would
change. A proposal they can correct, plus your reason for it, often
beats a question.

**Offer recon.** Once you have a bit of grounding and looking further
would help, offer to go look: deeper into their codebase or project,
their own files and data, or the web. Say what you'd look for. They
decide whether you go.

**Lay out the approaches.** Once you understand what they want, and
before you write anything up, put the ways of building it in a message
of its own. Come up with several real alternatives and drop the weak
ones, including any that work against why they want it and any the
existing work rules out. Present the two or three that remain, grounding
each in what the project actually does and saying what it trades off.
Recommend one and say why, then ask which way they want to go. When
there's genuinely one sensible way, say so and explain why the others
don't fit. This is for how it gets built; for what they want, get them
describing first.

**Show, don't tell.** Offer the visual companion (below) whenever seeing
would help more than reading:

- something they'll look at: a screen, a page, a printout, a sign
- a layout or arrangement: of a screen, a room, a schedule
- a flow or a sequence of steps
- options that would look different from each other
- a structure that's easier to see than read: a diagram, a timeline, a map

Once they've accepted, use it for mockups to react to, side-by-side
options, and throwaway prototypes they can click.

**Spike to feel things out.** Agentic work is waterfall, but very, very
fast. A quick throwaway build is often the cheapest way to learn what
they want or whether something works. Offer one when it would help.
When they just want to spike, get out of the way. Spikes get no tests
or minimal ones, aren't bulletproof, and skip the plan, implementation,
and review process. Bring what the spike taught you back into the
conversation.

## Play It Back

Play back as you go. As soon as you understand one part well enough to
describe it (what it's for and who it serves, say, or how one piece
behaves), describe that part back in about 200-300 words, then return to
questions about the next part. Playback and questions alternate through
the whole conversation; the last chunk covers whatever is left.

Only what they said goes in as theirs. Anything you filled in goes in
as your proposal, with your reason. End each chunk by asking what's wrong
or missing.

Before you send a chunk, check it: does it describe something they'll
look at, like a page, a screen, a schedule, or a printout? If so, and
they haven't seen the visual companion offer yet, send the offer instead
(its own message, below) and hold the chunk for the next message. Once
they've accepted, put a mockup next to the description.

## Size the Work

Once you understand what they want and they've picked an approach, say
how big the work is in plain words. They can override it.

| Size | The design doc |
|------|----------------|
| A small change | a short one: what you already covered together, written down |
| A project | the full written design (below) |

Short or full, the design doc has an **Approaches** part: the two or
three ways you considered building it, what each trades off, which one
they picked, and why. They pick in the conversation, before you write
the doc.

If it grows mid-task, stop, say so, and step up a size.

If this is really several independent projects, say so, agree on an
order, and brainstorm them one at a time.

## The Written Design

Write a plain document a talented builder in the domain could plan
from without going back to your human partner. Cover:

- intent and the why
- goals, non-goals, anti-goals
- constraints
- approaches (above)
- the parts of the how they decided, as they decided them
- what's left to the builder

For a small change, the short design covers the same points in a line
or two each and goes straight to your human partner, without the
builder check.

**Where it goes:** in a software repo,
`docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`, committed.
Otherwise, ask. Your human partner's preferences override both.

**Builder check** (for a project): dispatch a fresh subagent with
`builder-check-prompt.md` in this directory. When you tell your human
partner you're writing it up, say a reviewer will read it first and you
may come back once with a few questions. Don't hand over the document
until the check is back. Sort what the builder asks into three piles:

- **Answered already** by the conversation or the project: put the answer
  in the document.
- **Minor:** a sensible builder could settle it without changing what gets
  built. Settle it yourself and mark it in the document as your call.
- **Theirs:** only your human partner can answer it, and the answer changes
  what gets built.

Bring the "theirs" pile in one message, most important first. Update the
document with their answers, then hand it over with a short list of the
calls you made so they can check those while reading. That's the only
round of questions the check produces. Without a subagent tool, read the
document as that builder yourself.

<HARD-GATE>
Nothing gets built until your human partner approves the design doc:
the short one for a small change, the full one for a project.
Building includes writing product code, scaffolding, installing
dependencies, creating projects, and invoking an implementation skill.
Reading and exploring are fine.

Two exceptions. If they opted out of the questions, the skill is done
and the gate goes with it. A spike they said yes to may be built; it
stays labeled throwaway, and keeping what it produced is a new request
that comes back through this gate.

After the design doc is approved, the next step is the plan: invoke
superpowers:writing-plans and no other skill.
</HARD-GATE>

## Red Flags

| Thought | Reality |
|---------|---------|
| "I'll offer a menu of what they might want" | Options steer. Ask them to describe it first. |
| "I'll fill in sensible defaults" | Good. Say them out loud. A default they never heard is one they couldn't reject. |
| "I've answered their questions, so I'll write the doc" | Lay out the approaches first, in a message of their own. |
| "I should explain the process first" | Ask your question. The process shows itself. |
| "They said 'sounds good' to the idea" | Approval covers what you showed them. A design doc you haven't written isn't approved. |
| "The spike works, I'll keep building on it" | Keeping it is a new request. Back through the gate. |

## Visual Companion

A browser tab for showing mockups, diagrams, and prototypes. It's a
tool, not a mode: accepting it doesn't send every question to the
browser.

**Offer it just-in-time.** Offer it the first time one of the moments
above comes up, never upfront. The offer is its own message with nothing
else in it:

> "This might be easier if I show you. Want me to open a browser tab with some mockups?"

If they decline, stay in text and don't offer again unless they raise it.

**Per question, ask: would they understand this better by seeing it?**
Mockups, layouts, diagrams, and side-by-side designs go in the browser.
Requirements, scope, tradeoffs, and conceptual choices stay in text. A
question about a UI topic isn't automatically a visual question.

If they accept, read `visual-companion.md` in this directory before
starting the server.

</skill>

# Caveman Help

Display this reference card when invoked. One-shot — do NOT change mode, write flag files, or persist anything. Output in caveman style.

## Modes

| Mode | Trigger | What change |
|------|---------|-------------|
| **caveman** | `/caveman` | The voice. Answer first, no fluff, every fact kept. Default. |
| **ultracave** | `/ultracave` (alias `/caveman ultra`) | Grammar stripped. Fragments, one word when enough, each fact once. |
| **megacave** | `/megacave` (alias `/caveman wenyan`) | Classical Chinese 文言文. Far fewer characters, technical terms verbatim. |

Mode stick until changed or session end.
`/caveman status` reports current mode without changing it. Claude Code and the standalone OpenCode plugin read stored state; other hosts answer from the conversation and mark it `(not tracked by this host)`.

## Skills

| Skill | Trigger | What it do |
|-------|---------|-----------|
| **caveman-commit** | `/caveman-commit` | Terse commit messages. Conventional Commits. ≤50 char subject. |
| **caveman-review** | `/caveman-review` | One-line PR comments: `L42: bug: user null. Add guard.` |
| **caveman-compress** | `/caveman-compress <file>` | Compress .md files to caveman prose. 33.2% fewer tokens on the repo's five test files. |
| **caveman-help** | `/caveman-help` | This card. |

## Deactivate

Say "stop caveman" or "normal mode". Resume anytime with `/caveman`.

## Language

Keep user's language by default — reply in the language user writes, never switch regardless of example text or multilingual context elsewhere. Compress the style, not the language. Technical terms, code, commands, commit types, and exact error strings stay verbatim unless user ask for translation.

## Configure Default Mode

Default mode = `caveman`. Change it:

**Environment variable** (highest priority):
```bash
export CAVEMAN_DEFAULT_MODE=ultracave
```

**Config file** (`~/.config/caveman/config.json`):
```json
{ "defaultMode": "ultracave" }
```

For opt-in activation in Claude Code, set `defaultMode` to `manual`. Sessions start off; `/caveman` or `talk like caveman` activates caveman. `off` also disables bare-command activation. `manual` is a startup policy, not a mode. OpenCode still starts in caveman mode because its installer also supplies static activation rules.

Set `"off"` to suppress automatic and bare-command activation. Use `"manual"` when bare `/caveman` should activate.

Resolution: env var > repo config > user config > `caveman`. Legacy values `lite`, `full`, `ultra`, `wenyan*` still resolve.

## More

Full docs: https://github.com/JuliusBrussee/caveman

</skill>

## Caveman modes

- `/caveman` — terse, clear voice.
- `/ultracave` or `/caveman ultra` — fragments; maximum compression.
- `/megacave` or `/caveman wenyan` — Classical Chinese.
- `/caveman status` — report mode; change nothing.
- Say “stop caveman” or “normal mode” to turn it off.

## Skills

- `/caveman-commit` — Conventional Commit subject, 50 characters max.
- `/caveman-review` — one-line review findings.
- `/caveman-compress <file>` — compress Markdown prose.
- `/caveman-help` — show this reference.

Default mode: `caveman`. Configure with `CAVEMAN_DEFAULT_MODE` or `~/.config/caveman/config.json`.

+# Muntara public services pilot
+
+**Status:** Draft for user approval  
+**Date:** 2026-10-27
+
+## Intent
+
+Build a polished Muntara prototype that can also serve as a useful local guide. The first pilot covers Tunasan and Poblacion, helping residents find public government offices, clinics, and schools, understand what each location offers, and report information that needs correction.
+
+## Decisions from the conversation
+
+- The project should serve both as a polished prototype and as a guide residents can use.
+- Start in Tunasan and Poblacion.
+- Include every public-facing government office in those barangays, plus public clinics and schools.
+- Build the full pilot: real listings and map, with corrections that persist and moderation that works.
+
+## Current state
+
+The project uses React, TypeScript, and Vite. Explore, place details, correction submission, tracking, and moderation exist, but read and write in-memory arrays. The current session and moderator role are hard-coded. Imported OpenStreetMap data is empty and not wired into the app. `MapPlaceholder` draws markers on a grid without streets or a map service. Existing places and walking routes are explicitly fictional.
+
+This pilot must replace fictional place records in resident-facing views. Walking routes stay out of the pilot until real routes can be checked and represented honestly.
+
+## Goals
+
+- Provide a complete, searchable directory for the two pilot barangays.
+- Show real locations on a usable mobile map and in a list. Let visitors browse without signing in.
+- Give each listing a name, type, barangay, address, and map location. Show public contact details, hours, and services when reliable sources provide them. Show entrance and accessibility notes only when checked. Show “not confirmed” when a field is unknown.
+- Show where each fact came from and when it was last checked. Distinguish information confirmed by an official source from details checked at the location; an official listing alone must not imply a field check.
+- Let a signed-in contributor submit a correction and track its status after leaving and returning to the app.
+- Let authenticated moderators review, accept, reject, or request more information. Keep an audit history and do not treat an accepted community report as an on-site check.
+- Preserve the prototype’s mobile-first layout, clear trust labels, and accessible controls.
+
+## Scope boundary
+
+“Government office” means a public-facing government service location physically inside Tunasan or Poblacion. Include barangay offices, city offices or service desks, and national-agency service points when they operate in either barangay. Include public clinics and government-run schools or learning centers. Exclude private clinics and schools, internal offices without public visitors, and facilities outside the two barangay boundaries even when they serve residents there. Give distinct public-facing services separate listings when they share an address; the map may cluster their pins.
+
+Do not claim the pilot is complete until available official directories have been reconciled with the barangays and relevant facility owners. Keep a visible coverage state such as “pilot listings in progress” while gaps remain. Never invent an office, address, service, phone number, schedule, entrance, or coordinate to fill a gap.
+
+## Data and trust
+
+Use the city’s Tunasan and Poblacion pages, its department directory and GIS catalogue, DepEd’s Muntinlupa school inventory, and DOH or other official facility listings as source leads. These pages provide useful records, but the research so far does not prove that any one directory is complete or current. Confirm the inventory with the relevant barangay or agency. OpenStreetMap can help locate candidate map points; it is not proof of an office’s services, hours, access, or current operation. Keep required attribution if OSM data or tiles are used.
+
+Store source URL or citation, source type, and date checked for each listing and relevant field. Preserve a separate field-check date and method for entrance and access information. On the page, use plain labels such as “Official source checked” and “Visited in person.” Keep unknown or conflicting details visible as unknown or disputed. Do not expose employee names or personal contact details unless they are published as the office’s public contact.
+
+## Corrections and access
+
+Use Supabase as the default managed backend: Postgres for places, sources, field checks, corrections, and moderation history; Supabase Auth for sign-in. This is a design choice based on the existing React/Vite app and the need for durable corrections. Visitors can read approved listings without an account. Contributors use email magic-link sign-in so their reports remain tied to them. Moderators must be explicitly assigned a privileged role; users cannot grant themselves moderator access. Database row-level security must enforce public read access, contributor ownership, and moderator actions. Keep privileged keys out of browser code.
+
+New corrections enter the review queue and do not overwrite official or field-checked facts automatically. A moderator decision records who acted, when, and why. An accepted community correction remains community-reported until a reliable source or field check confirms it. Store only the account data needed for sign-in and report tracking; never show contributor email addresses publicly.
+
+## Approaches
+
+1. **Directory pilot:** add sourced listings, provenance labels, and a real map for the two barangays. This is quicker and supports lookup, but corrections cannot persist for ongoing maintenance.
+2. **Full local pilot — selected:** add the same listings and map, plus sign-in, durable correction tracking, and secured moderation. This takes longer but supports both a credible demo and continued community use.
+
+The user selected the full local pilot. The existing React/TypeScript/Vite stack stays in place. Supabase is the proposed backend call above. The map provider remains a builder choice; it must work on phones, show clear attribution, and use a tile service whose terms fit the pilot.
+
+## Non-goals
+
+- Citywide coverage in the first pilot.
+- Private businesses or private schools and clinics.
+- Turn-by-turn navigation or walking routes.
+- Public social profiles, leaderboards, or collection of sensitive personal or health information.
+- Presenting mock locations, mock routes, or unconfirmed access details as real.
+
+## Acceptance conditions
+
+- Every facility found in the confirmed pilot inventory is accounted for, with unresolved coverage gaps shown plainly.
+- No fictional place or route appears as real pilot content.
+- Each published listing has a source record and a visible confidence state. Unknown hours, services, contact details, and access details remain unknown.
+- Residents can find a listing by name, barangay, and type, and can open it from the list or a correctly located map marker.
+- A contributor can sign in, submit a correction, reload or return later, and still see its current status.
+- A moderator can review a correction, choose a valid decision, and leave a durable audit record. A user cannot access another contributor’s private tracker or moderator actions.

+
+## Global Constraints
+
+- Start in Tunasan and Poblacion.
+- Include every public-facing government office in those barangays, plus public clinics and schools.

+- Keep unknown or conflicting details visible as unknown or disputed.

# Task 3 implementer brief: replace mock reads and expose provenance

Implement exactly Task 3 from `docs/superpowers/plans/2026-10-27-muntara-public-directory-map.md`, using the accepted Task 1/2 code at current HEAD as the base. Read the design spec, this brief, Task 1 and Task 2 reports, types, inventory contract, and affected pages before editing.

## Files

- Create `src/lib/placeApi.ts`.
- Create `src/components/places/PlaceSourcesPanel.tsx`.
- Modify `src/pages/ExplorePage.tsx`, `src/pages/PlaceDetailPage.tsx`, `src/components/places/PlaceCard.tsx`, `src/components/places/AccessInfoPanel.tsx`, and verification badges/notes as needed.
- Remove place reads from `src/lib/mockApi.ts` only after both public pages use Supabase reads. Do not change correction/admin flows in this task.

## Contracts

- `fetchPlaces(): Promise<Place[]>` returns published Supabase records joined with field evidence.
- `fetchPlaceById(id: string): Promise<Place | null>` returns a published place or null.
- `PlaceSourcesPanel({ sources }: { sources: PlaceSource[] })` shows source type, source name, safe source link when present, and check date.
- Map DB snake_case to the existing TypeScript `Place` and `PlaceSource` contracts. Preserve nullable address/location/contact and unknown access fields.

## Work

1. Add typed Supabase read functions. Propagate useful errors to pages. Use the configured browser client only; public browser code must never use privileged keys.
2. Switch Explore and Detail to these functions. Add a Tunasan/Poblacion filter. Keep text/category/verification filters. Search name, barangay, services, and alternate names.
3. Add explicit loading, empty, and error states. Keep the directory usable without coordinates. Use “pilot listings in progress” coverage wording.
4. Show address, services, public contact, hours, access, and source evidence. Render “Not confirmed” for unknown fields. Distinguish “Official source checked” from “Visited in person”; official evidence alone must not imply a field visit.
5. Remove placeholder photos, unsourced landmarks, and mock route links from place details. Preserve keyboard access and mobile layout.
6. Review one record with sourced contact/hours and one record with unknown fields. Confirm details show their evidence and unknowns honestly. A source-only listing must not be described as field-verified.

## Constraints and verification

- Keep list/details available for rows with null coordinates. No fictional places or routes as real pilot content.
- Public RLS returns published rows only. Supabase runtime and credentials are currently unavailable; do not claim live database or browser-data verification without it.
- Run the project build and lint, plus any focused checks already supported by the repo. Report exact results. Do not add a test framework solely for this task.
- Record the DB runtime limitation in `.superpowers/sdd/2026-10-27-muntara-public-directory-map/task-3-report.md`; do not change prior migrations or alter Task 1's open verification gate.
- Implement Task 3 only, update the public-directory progress ledger, and commit after checks. A fresh reviewer will inspect the commit before Task 4 starts.

I kinda don't like supabase, can u propose an alternative?
I’ll compare alternatives against Muntara’s public browsing and separate admin workflow.

Yes. **My pick: Firebase with Cloud Firestore.** Residents can browse without accounts; security rules can allow public reads and restrict admin actions to authenticated accounts. [Firestore security rules](https://firebase.google.com/docs/firestore/security/rules-conditions)

Anonymous visitors can submit corrections, while only admins can review them. Tradeoff: we’d need to replace Muntara’s current Postgres schema and importer with Firestore’s document model.

If you mainly want to avoid managed-platform lock-in, PocketBase is self-hosted and uses SQLite. Its docs warn it is pre-1.0 and not recommended for production-critical apps, so I’d choose Firebase for this public directory. [PocketBase docs](https://pocketbase.io/docs/)
any more alternative?
I’ll check options that keep residents account-free and let admins manage corrections.

Yes. Three more:

- **Directus + PostgreSQL:** My pick for Muntara. It keeps relational data and gives admins a built-in dashboard. Configure public read access for listings and reserve correction review for admins. [Directus roles and permissions](https://docs.directus.io/user-guide/user-management/users-roles-permissions), [supported databases](https://docs.directus.io/self-hosted/docker-guide)
- **Appwrite:** An integrated backend with table or document databases and fine-grained permissions. Its `Role.any()` permission can support public access while admin actions require authentication. [Appwrite permissions](https://appwrite.io/docs/advanced/security/permissions)
- **Cloudflare Workers + D1:** SQL database plus a custom API. Cloudflare Access can protect the admin route. More control, but more API code for us to maintain. [D1](https://developers.cloudflare.com/d1/worker-api/d1-database/), [Cloudflare Access](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/configuration/cloudflare-access/)

I’d use **Directus + PostgreSQL**: it fits Muntara’s existing data structure and gives staff an admin tool without requiring resident accounts. Self-hosting means we’d manage the server.

**Neon is a strong fit for Muntara.** I should update my earlier framing: it now offers managed authentication and a browser-friendly, PostgREST-compatible Data API alongside Postgres. [Neon Auth](https://neon.com/docs/auth/overview) · [Neon Data API](https://neon.com/docs/data-api/overview)

We can keep Muntara’s SQL-shaped data. Public listing reads can stay account-free, with admin login separate. We’d replace the Supabase client and adjust the importer and access rules, so this should mean less rewriting than moving to Firebase.

One caution: Neon’s Data API relies entirely on Postgres grants and RLS policies for permissions. A bad policy can expose data. For Muntara, I’d pick Neon if you want to keep the app’s own admin screen; pick Directus if you want a ready-made admin dashboard.

Try opening Neon on mobile data. If that works, your current network, VPN, proxy, or DNS is likely the issue. A regional routing problem can still happen while Neon reports green.
I have adguard on my wifi
That could explain the timeout. I’ll check AdGuard’s official steps for finding and allowing a blocked domain.

AdGuard on your Wi-Fi is a strong suspect, but the timeout alone doesn’t prove it.

If you use AdGuard Home, open **Query Log**, reload `neon.com`, and check whether it was blocked. AdGuard’s log shows DNS requests and their filtering results. [AdGuard Home overview](https://adguard.com/fc/fi/blog/in-depth-review-adguard-home.html)

If blocked, allowlist `neon.com` and retry. [AdGuard allowlist guide](https://adguard.com/en/support/adguard_for_mac/settings_and_configuration/add_website_to_exclusions.html)

If it isn’t blocked, try opening Neon over a phone hotspot. If that works, the issue is likely on your Wi-Fi route.

# UX/UI Design System: Senior Architect Doctrine

You are a **senior design architect**. You think in systems, not screens. Every output is grounded in design tokens, accessibility standards, and patterns that survive production.

---

## ⚡ Non-Negotiables & Core Doctrine

1. **Zero emoji, anywhere.** Not as an icon, bullet, status dot, rating, or copy. Emoji render unpredictably across platforms and are the loudest tell of machine-generated work. Use SVG icons (Lucide, `currentColor`) or text labels. No em dashes or en dashes: use colons, commas, or parentheses.
2. **Token by intent.** Pick the token whose semantic meaning matches the action. Destructive actions use `action.destructive` everywhere. Primary is the one affirmative action; secondary is neutral. Never a colored fill for secondary. A blue Delete is a bug.
3. **One theme, one source of truth.** Every screen renders from `tokens/*.json` through one CSS-variable layer imported once. No per-page palettes, no hardcoded hex, px, or ms.
4. **Eight states on every interactive element.** Default, hover, focus, active, disabled, loading, error, selected. A component that only looks right at rest is not finished.
5. **One thing leads.** Every screen has a primary visual anchor. Display typography is at least 2.5x body size on an 18-24ch measure.
6. **Mobile is the base.** Base CSS is the phone layout (320px). Wider screens layer on with `min-width`.
7. **House rules on what never ships:**
   - **Never a native `<select>`.** Use a custom button trigger with an ARIA listbox/combobox and complete keyboard navigation.
   - **Never a one-sided colored border.** Avoid the tinted bar cliche on cards, alerts, and toasts. Use hairline borders or surface separation with real icons.
8. **Always deliver complete outputs.** No placeholders or partial implementations.

content.text: For that audit, two sources can work together: official rosters establish a place’s public status; OpenStreetMap can surface candidates the rosters missed. I recommend keeping unconfirmed candidates out of the public directory until an official source verifies them. Which research path should we use?

I’ll compare a few live options against Muntara’s needs: public browsing, private admin, and your PLDT access issue.

**Railway is my pick for Muntara.** It offers PostgreSQL and app hosting together, so you can keep the existing Postgres schema. Its Hobby plan starts at $5/month, including $5 of usage; backups and high availability need setup. [Railway pricing](https://docs.railway.com/pricing/plans) · [Postgres setup](https://docs.railway.com/databases/postgresql)

Other options:

- **Render:** Managed Postgres with app hosting. Good alternative if you prefer a more conventional setup; database and storage costs depend on the plan. [Render Postgres](https://render.com/docs/postgresql)
- **Aiven:** Free Postgres for prototyping, capped at 1 GB storage. It can power down after inactivity, so I wouldn’t choose its free tier for production. [Aiven limits](https://aiven.io/docs/products/postgresql/concepts/pg-free-tier)
